title: Nvidia Denies Report It Is Rolling Out China AI Chip by Year-End
excerpt: The chipmaker says a report claiming it plans to ship a language processing unit for Chinese customers is incorrect and no such product is on its roadmap.
body:
• Nvidia has denied a report by The Information claiming it plans to ship a language processing unit (LPU) tailored for Chinese customers by year-end.
  • The company said it has no LPU sales in China and no China-specific LPU product on its roadmap.
  • The report claimed the chip uses technology licensed from startup Groq and complied with U.S. export-control rules.
  • CEO Jensen Huang said in May that Nvidia had "largely conceded" China's AI chip market to Huawei Technologies.

Nvidia Pushes Back on LPU Report

Nvidia on Thursday issued a flat denial of a report that it is developing and preparing to ship an artificial intelligence chip specifically designed for Chinese customers, calling the claims "incorrect" and insisting no such product exists on its roadmap.

"The reporting in The Information on Nvidia's LPU is incorrect. We have no LPU sales in the China market today, and no China-specific LPU product in our roadmap," an Nvidia spokesperson said.

The Information had reported earlier Thursday, citing two Nvidia employees, that the company planned to begin small-batch shipments of a language processing unit — a processor developed using technology licensed from startup Groq — designed for Chinese customers by the end of 2026. The publication said several customers had already placed orders.

What the Report Claimed

According to The Information, the chip was a version of Nvidia's LPU that works alongside graphics processing units to speed up AI chatbot responses. The publication reported that the chip complied with U.S. export-control rules, and that Nvidia had modified software to allow the LPU to operate with processors available in China after its next-generation Vera Rubin AI system became unavailable to the Chinese market because of Washington's restrictions.

Reuters had separately reported in March that Nvidia was preparing a China-compatible version of AI chips as it sought to compete in the fast-growing market for AI inference — the process of running trained AI models to generate responses.

"The reporting in The Information on Nvidia's LPU is incorrect. We have no LPU sales in the China market today, and no China-specific LPU product in our roadmap."

— Nvidia spokesperson

A Market Nvidia Has 'Largely Conceded'

Nvidia's China business has been in flux amid an escalating technology war between Washington and Beijing. The U.S. government in May approved sales of Nvidia's H200 AI chips to a limited group of Chinese firms including Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance, though deliveries only recently began. Nvidia has also been marketing its Vera CPU to Chinese customers.

CEO Jensen Huang had acknowledged in May that Nvidia had "largely conceded" China's AI chip market to Huawei Technologies, which has emerged as the company's main domestic rival. Huawei's Ascend series of AI processors has gained significant traction among Chinese tech companies facing restrictions on importing advanced American semiconductors.

The denial comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia, which remains the world's most valuable chipmaker and the primary beneficiary of the global AI infrastructure buildout. Any move to supply China-specific chips would draw intense scrutiny from U.S. regulators who have repeatedly tightened export controls to prevent advanced AI hardware from reaching Chinese military and surveillance applications.

What to Watch

The conflicting signals around Nvidia's China strategy reflect the broader uncertainty facing U.S. semiconductor companies navigating between commercial opportunity and national security restrictions. With the AI inference market growing rapidly in China and Huawei filling the gap left by U.S. export controls, Nvidia faces a strategic dilemma: cede the market entirely or develop compliant products that can pass regulatory scrutiny. The company's emphatic denial suggests it is not currently pursuing the latter path, though the competitive pressure from Huawei is unlikely to ease.
